rationale: This is the archive's leading kinked-financing signal with the sole change of a one-year-lagged asset deflator — a cosmetic measurement variant whose economic content is identical, and since both the financing flow and the quality leg are re-scaled by the same lagged base, the cross-sectional ranks will be near-collinear with the original, so the test has little power to teach anything new.

target_name: Financing per unit of internal funds
rationale: The construction is internally inconsistent with its own justification — ABS(oancf) gives a large *negative*-cash-flow firm a large denominator, so the deepest cash burners are scored as having the most "internal funds capacity," exactly inverting the intended quality tilt — and stripped of that flaw the signal is simply the well-known net external financing anomaly with an unstable, near-zero-prone deflator.

Adding financing-policy consistency to the credibility weight is an economically distinct and defensible upgrade to the leading kink structure rather than a rescaling, though the reviewer should note that five-year financing volatility is mechanically correlated with the magnitude of the current financing flow, so the weight will systematically shrink precisely the largest observations in both legs.

This is literally a sub-expression of the already-evaluated channel-specific kink (and a close relative of the gen-0 quality-gated net payout), so it is an ablation diagnostic rather than a new signal, and its result is largely predictable from the two existing tests that already bracket it.

This is the sign-flipped version of the gen-3 working-capital signal that failed at t=−2.64, re-rationalized after the fact, and the claim that the current-ratio change is "not mechanically linked to the financing inflow" is wrong — issuance proceeds land in current assets, so the signal largely reduces to going long the biggest raisers, contradicting the well-documented external-financing effect.

The stated logic contradicts the expression: RANK(NEG(sales growth)) is *largest* for shrinking firms, so capital-returning shrinking firms occupy the extreme long leg rather than being "scored near neutral," meaning the trade is driven by a different (and less defensible) economic claim than the hypothesis states, on top of being close to the known net-external-financing/asset-growth complex.
